questions.topic: Partial sums that never settle

questions.stem: For the series 1 - 1 + 1 - 1 with all further alternating terms, a number line is drawn and the partial sums are marked on it as dots: the first dot sits at 1, the second at 0, the third back at 1, the fourth at 0, and the two marked positions repeat as far as the line extends. options.misconception: reads the first partial sum as though it were the limit

options.text: The series sums to 0, because the two marked positions sit symmetrically and must therefore cancel

options.text: The series sums to 1/2, because the midpoint of the two marked positions is where the dots ought to settle

options.text: The series diverges, because the marked partial sums never approach a single position however far the line extends

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: What a radius of convergence guarantees
questions.learningObjective: state precisely the region in which a power series equals its function
questions.stem: A function f has a power series representation about a point a with radius of convergence R. What does that representation guarantee?

options.text: The series converges to f(x) at the two endpoints |x - a| = R, because a radius bounds the interior and says nothing about them
options.misconception: reads silence about the endpoints as a guarantee of convergence there

options.text: The series is only an approximation to f(x) wherever it converges, never an exact equality
options.misconception: believes a convergent power series is a mere approximation rather than an identity

options.text: The series converges to f(x) at every real x with |x - a| strictly below R, and asserts nothing at or beyond it
The series converges to f(x) for every real x, since an exact power series representation is valid at all points
options.misconception: assumes a Taylor representation extends to the whole real line

questions.explanation: A power series is a statement about a region, and the region is the open interval of radius R about the centre a. Inside it the partial sums converge to f, which is the content of the coefficient-matching argument that proves every power series analytic, and the limit is pointwise. At the endpoints and beyond nothing is asserted: the series may converge to f, may converge to something else, or may fail to converge at all, and each of those behaviours occurs for real functions of this kind. The safe formulation is that the representation holds strictly inside the radius and claims nothing outside it, which is why every radius computation is followed by two endpoint tests.
questions.hint: Separate what is proved, the equality inside the open interval, from what is merely undecided at the boundary.

options.misconception: reads a stalled test limit as a positive verdict

options.text: Nothing at all, since a limit of 1 means the radius of 2 was computed incorrectly and must be rechecked
options.misconception: concludes the radius is in doubt when only the endpoints are undecided

options.text: Only that the series is undecided at those two points, each of which needs its own test before an interval can be written down

questions.explanation: Both tests settle an open region and go silent exactly on the boundary, because a limit of 1 is shared by series that converge, that diverge, and that oscillate there. So the radius of 2 is established as far as either test can establish it, and the interval of convergence still needs the two endpoint tests, whose outcomes may agree or disagree with each other. Reading a stalled limit as a verdict in either direction is the most common error at this step.
questions.hint: Ask what the ratio test can and cannot conclude when its limit is exactly one, and compare two series that share that limit.

questions.topic: Uniform convergence on a closed subinterval
questions.learningObjective: identify the subintervals on which a power series converges uniformly
questions.stem: A power series centred at 0 has radius of convergence 3. What can be said about its convergence on the closed interval from -1 to 1?

It converges uniformly there only if the coefficients happen to vanish at the ends, which they need not

options.text: It converges uniformly there and also on the closed interval from -3 to 3, since both intervals meet the radius
options.misconception: treats an interval reaching the boundary as uniformly convergent

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Passing a limit through a sum
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of uniform convergence in interchanging a limit and an infinite sum
questions.stem: Explain why a limit may be taken through an infinite summation sign when the series of functions converges uniformly, and give a concrete example of what goes wrong when it does not.

answer.exemplar: Taking a limit term by term is justified precisely when the error left by the finite partial sums is small for every point of the interval at once, not merely small at each point separately. If the functions f_n on [a, b] converge uniformly to f, then for some N the tail sup-norm is below any epsilon we like, so the finite sum up to N can be passed through the limit with an error that vanishes, and the interchange is legitimate. Without uniformity the error may be small at each fixed x but large at points that move as N grows, and the interchange then fails. The standard example is f_n(x) = x^n on the interval from 0 to 1. Every f_n tends to 0 at each fixed x below 1, so the sum of the pointwise limits is 0, whereas the sum of the series at such an x is x over (1 - x), which is not 0, so the interchange already fails on the whole interior of the interval; at the single endpoint the situation is worse, because there the terms are all 1 and the partial sums run off without bound, so the limit of the sums does not exist at all. A second example shows the summation itself breaking: take the series 1 - 1 + 1 - 1 with all further terms, whose partial sums alternate between 1 and 0, so no limit of partial sums exists and nothing can be interchanged at all.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to give the failure mode, not merely assert that uniformity suffices, so the response names the moving bad point in the x^n example and notes that a series without a limit at all supports no interchange whatsoever.
questions.hint: Compare the size of the tail of the series at one fixed point with the largest size it reaches anywhere on the interval.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Rearranging a conditionally convergent series
questions.learningObjective: explain why order matters for conditional but not for absolute convergence
questions.stem: Explain why rearranging the terms of a conditionally convergent series can change its sum, while rearranging an absolutely convergent series cannot, and state the standard result about how much the sum can be moved.

answer.exemplar: The distinction is about the tails, not about the terms. For an absolutely convergent series the sum of the positive terms and the sum of the negative terms are each finite, so any ordering draws from two fixed finite pools and the partial sums of the new ordering stay close to the same total; in the limit the order is invisible. For a conditionally convergent series the positive terms alone diverge to infinity and the negative terms alone diverge to minus infinity, so the value of the sum is decided entirely by how the two divergent pools are interleaved, and a different interleaving gives a different balance. Because the two pools are both infinite, one can arrange a new ordering in which the positive terms are used up far enough ahead to push the partial sums past any prescribed value, and then the ordering can be completed so they stay above it, which forces the sum to be larger than the original; the mirror construction forces it to be smaller. The standard result is that by suitable rearrangement a conditionally convergent series can be made to sum to any real number at all, and to diverge to plus or minus infinity, whereas the sum of an absolutely convergent series is fixed by the order-independent total of the absolute values. The alternating harmonic series 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 with all further terms, which sums to the logarithm of 2, is the standard example to rearrange.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to explain the mechanism in terms of the two divergent sub-pools rather than assert the theorem, since the bare statement that the sum can be changed does not show why the order enters at all.
questions.hint: Compare the sum of the positive terms and the sum of the negative terms in the two cases, and ask which is finite.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: The integral form of the remainder
questions.learningObjective: state the integral form of the Taylor remainder and explain when it is the better tool
questions.stem: State the integral form of the remainder in Taylor's theorem, and explain why it is more informative than the Lagrange form in one specific situation.

answer.exemplar: Taylor's theorem says that for a function f with n+1 continuous derivatives on an interval containing a and x, there is a point c strictly between a and x such that f(x) equals its degree-n Taylor polynomial at a plus f to the (n+1) power of c over (n+1) factorial, times (x - a) to the (n+1) power; that is the Lagrange form, and it is useful because it gives a single number bounding the error. The integral form writes the same remainder as 1 over n factorial times the integral from a to x of f to the (n+1) power of t times (x - t) to the power n, and the same identity follows by integrating the (n+1)st derivative once and applying the fundamental theorem of the calculus. The integral form earns its keep in exactly one situation: determining the sign of the remainder. The kernel (x - t)^n has a constant sign on the interval, so the sign of the remainder is the sign of the integrand, that is the sign of the (n+1)st derivative throughout, provided it does not change sign. The Lagrange form cannot deliver that, because the point c it names is an unknown interior point and the derivative may behave differently at c than elsewhere. For example, the remainder of the first-degree Taylor polynomial of the cosine at 0 is the integral of minus cosine over the interval, which is negative because the cosine is positive there, so the tangent line overestimates; the same conclusion from the Lagrange form would require knowing the sign of minus cosine at an unnamed interior point.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to pin down the one situation named in the stem, the sign of the remainder, and show why the constant-sign kernel is what delivers it, rather than merely presenting both formulas side by side.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two forms leaves the derivative evaluated at a point you cannot pin down, and which keeps it visible across an interval.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Why the sum claim stops at the radius
questions.learningObjective: explain why a power series represents its function only inside the radius
questions.stem: Explain why a power series is only asserted to equal the function it came from inside its radius of convergence, and describe what can happen once the series is continued past that radius.

answer.exemplar: A power series is a limit of partial sums of polynomials, and a polynomial is defined at every real x, so the series is a well-defined object everywhere it converges. But convergence is a property of the coefficients, not of the function, and it is controlled entirely by how fast the coefficients grow: a coefficient sequence that decays like the reciprocal of a power forces a finite radius, because beyond that distance the individual terms fail to shrink to zero. The identity with the original function is a separate statement, proved inside the radius by matching coefficients, and it does not travel further on its own. Three behaviours are possible outside. The series may continue to converge and agree with the function, as the exponential series does at every real x because its radius is infinite. It may converge to a different value, as the geometric series does at x = 3, where the closed form 1 over (1 - x) returns a value that is the function's value while the series itself has no sum at all, since its terms are 3^n. It may converge to the function's own analytic continuation, the case that makes the theory deep, as with the reciprocal of 1 + x squared, which is perfectly well defined for every real x, and whose analytic continuation from the interval where its series converges does take the function's values out on the whole real axis even though the series itself diverges for every modulus of x above 1, since the radius is pinned by the complex poles at the imaginary unit and its negative. What the radius forbids is any blanket claim, and that is why every question about a series at a point asks first whether the point is inside the radius.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to separate the two independent issues, where the series converges and where it equals the function, and then show the outside-the-radius cases concretely, since a vague reference to analytic continuation would not answer the question asked.
questions.hint: Ask separately whether the series converges there and whether it equals the function there; the answers can differ.
